### Linguistic Metadata

Our genetic data was taken from a range of sources (see Supplementary Table X <!--# This will be a table of where the samples were taken -->). In each case. there was a variant of the question "What is your primary language?". In Y cases, language was inferred based on the location from which the sample was taken. All coding decisions on language names, locations, and the comparability of questions across samples are detailed in the script `processing/format_geneticdata.R`.

In the tables below, we list some summary statistics. A notable discrepancy is that there are more individuals with missing language families than missing languages. In three cases, respondents gave an answer of a language, but we cannot pair it to a language from existing databases. These are: Imani (n = 19), Eyagu (n = 1), and Kora (n = 1).

```{r metadata, echo=FALSE}
options(knitr.kable.NA = '')
if(!file.exists("processed_data/genetic_samples.csv")){
  system("RScript processing/format_geneticdata.R")
}

# Make taxa labels

## Counts of
```

Linguistic decisions of note:

-   Paiwaian (n = 52) is a language which has disputed membership to TNG, and could also be considered as part of the Tereban family [@pawley2017]. We include this language as a branch of TNG.

```         
::: {.callout-note}
We could consider Paiwaian as Tereban. SP needs to talk to NE about the strength of evidence for doing this. 
```

-   We have one speaker of Orokolo, an Eleman language that is sometimes categorised as a TNG language. @pawley2017 write there is no evidence for this link. We do not categorise this language as TNG.

# Phylogenetic Results

## Genetic Data

This project leverages existing samples drawn from 14 papers, with an additional 7 unpublished samples. In total, we analyse a sample of 861 mitogenomes. See Supplementary Table XX for the original papers which details the sequencing technology used for each paper.

mtDNA samples were sequenced using \[what technology?\] <!--# How was this done? Probably ask Franois-Xavier -->. Sequences are reconstructed from the Revised Cambridge Reference Sequence (rCRS). See script `processing/create_reference_genomes.R` for processing details. We split mtDNA samples into M and N haplotype groups for computational efficiency.

```{r genetic_data_processing, echo = FALSE, eval=FALSE}
if(!file.exists("processed_data/papua_n.fasta") & 
   !file.exists("processed_data/papua_m.fasta")){
  system("RScript processing/create_reference_genomes.R")  
}
```

### Duplicate mitogenomes

There are 190 individuals with duplicate mtDNA mutations that group in to 107 distinct sets (i.e. some individuals have identical mitogenomes to multiple people). Of the 107 duplicate sets, 53 have mismatched language groupings.

For phylogenetic modelling, we do not include duplicate genomes, as the contain no additional information. We pick individuals at random.

## Phylogenetic model

We use BEAST v2.7.4 to infer the genealogical relationships between our set of XXX mitogenomes. We use the BEAST package bModeltest to assess the most appropriate Substitution model. bModeltest will switch between all Transistion and transversion models, providing the model average across the runs and means we do not need to commit to a particular substitution model.

We use a Coalescent Extended Bayesian Skyline Population history model (EBSP). The EBSP model leverages coalescent theory to account for fluctuating population size in the phylogenetic model, at multiple loci [@heled2008]. The sparsity of historical knowledge in Southern New Guinea means we do not have a good understanding of changes in population size. We opt for using a model that will allow for a fluctuating population, rather than assuming that it did not fluctuate. We adjust the factor rate of the tree prior to 0.5, and chnge the population prior mean to an improper prior of 1/x, as suggested in @heled2008.

For the M haplogroup data, the TIM model (Transition model, AC=GT, AT=CG and unequal base freq: 123341) was the most commonly implemented (45%). Gamma and Invariant site parameters were always present, with the Gamma shape estimated to 1.016, and 87.9% of all sites were invariant.

-   MCMC convergence is not great for M

-   It may be because I put two identical monophyletic constraints in. I have run again (02/07/2024) to see if this fixes the wobbly MCMC Chain

For the N haplogroup data, the TPM2 (AC=AT, AG=CT, CG=GT and equal base freq.: 121323) model was the most commonly implemented (23.11%). This was closely followed by the K80 or K2P model (121121, 21.92%). Gamma and Invariant site parameters were always present, with the Gamma shape estimated to 0.964, and 91.1% of all sites were invariant.

In each of the M and N Haplogroup trees, we have one outlier from the opposing group, which is labelled as a monphyletic outlier in the analysis. In addition we imposed monophyletic groupings for the B4a1 and P haplogroups within the N phylogeny. Within the M phylogeny, we impost monophyletic groupings for E, Q and M haplogroups. Additionally, within M we create monophyletic groups for M27, M28, and M29.

#### Clock model / Mutation Rates

We use a strict clock mutation rate for M and N haplogroups. We determine mtDNA mutations rates from studies calibrating the human mitochondrial clock (@rieux2014, @fu2013). In both studies we consider the whole genome substitution rate. We take the mean mutation rate from both papers to determine our rate.

|             Paper | Estimated Mean Mutation Rate |  Estimated 95% C.I.   |
|------------------:|:----------------------------:|:---------------------:|
|    Fu et al. 2013 |        2.67 x 10^-8^         | 2.16 - 3.16 x 10^-8^  |
| Rieux et al. 2014 |        2.143 x 10^-8^        | 1.58 - 2.706 x 10^-8^ |
|         Used here |       2.4065 x 10^-8^        |          \-           |

#### MCMC Settings

We run all models for 10,000,000 MCMC iterations, storing every 10,000 iterations. All necessary parameters have a ESS \> 200. We run the analyses twice to assess chain convergence. We take a burn-in of 20% <!--# check -->, which leaves us with a posterior sample of 8,000 trees for the M and N haplotypes, using the BEAST2 LogCombiner tool. We create a Maximum Clade Credibility tree (MCCT) using the BEAST2 TreeAnnotator tool [@heled2013].

# Inference Results

## Language Metadata

As set out above, we have divided the genetic data into major haplogroups, M & N, for phylogenetic analysis. The aim of this project is to determine whether linguistic affiliation structures genetic diversity by calculating the probability of sharing a language trait within a genetic clade, and the rate of within and between group variance for all pairs of traits. Traits are analysed at two levels, whether the language spoken by an individual is Trans-New Guinea of not, and then breaking Trans-New Guinea speakers down into language clades. This means for the two analyses, we have four results.

1.  M Haplogroup - Presence or absence of TNG
2.  M Haplogroup - Language Clade
3.  N Haplogroup - Presence or absence of TNG
4.  N Haplogroup - Language Clade

```{r m_haplogroup_data, eval=FALSE, echo=FALSE}
# Read in the M Haplotype tree
mtree_file = "NCI/20240704_M_CBES_bModelTest/CBES_bModeltest-papua_m.noburnin.trees"
m_tree = read.nexus(mtree_file)

# 31 individuals are N Haplotypes but do not have language data
# metadata %>%
#   filter(haplogroup_MN == "M" & PhyID %in% m_tree[[1]]$tip.label) %>%
#   # Remove missing langauge or responses that refer to unknown language.
#   filter(interview_language %in% c("", "Imani")) %>%
#   nrow()

metadata_m = metadata %>% 
  filter(haplogroup_MN == "M" & PhyID %in% m_tree[[1]]$tip.label) %>%
  filter(!interview_language %in% c("", "Imani")) %>%
  # Remove missing langauge or responses that refer to unknown language.
  select(ID, PhyID, interview_language, TNG_Branch, TNG, latitude_hybrid, longitude_hybrid)

metadata_m = rbind(metadata_m, metadata[metadata$PhyID == "HGDP00546_P1d(P1d1a)",
                                      c("ID", "PhyID", "interview_language", 
                                        "TNG_Branch", "TNG", "latitude_hybrid", 
                                        "longitude_hybrid")])

# Prune the tree for all individuals for which we have language data for
keep_tips = metadata_m$PhyID

cat("There are", length(m_tree[[1]]$tip.label),"taxa in the N Haplogroup phylogeny")

m_tree = lapply(m_tree, function(t)
  keep.tip(t, keep_tips))

cat("There are", length(keep_tips),"language matched taxa in the M Haplogroup phylogeny")

ape::write.nexus(m_tree, 
                 file = paste0("NCI/20240618_R_M/",  basename(mtree_file)))

tt = assert_that(nrow(metadata_m) > 1)

write.csv(metadata_m, "NCI/20240618_R_M/language_metadata.csv")
```

### Trait heritage

To estimate the fidelity of language transmission over time, we calculate the probability of two individuals sharing a language within a genetic clade, across multiple times point in the phylogenetic history. This calculation follow from [@lansing2017].

$$
P(i_l,j_l)|i_{g(t)}, j_{g(t)}) = \frac{P(i_l, j_l \bigcap i_{g(t)}, j_{g(t)})}{P(i_{g(t)}, j_{g(t)}} = \frac{\sum_{g=1}^{c_t}(\sum_{i,j\neq i}1_{cos(l_ig, l_jg) > 0})}{\sum_{g=1}^{c_t}n_g(n_g - 1) / 2}
$$

$c_t$ is the number of genetic clades at any point in history, for t generations. We assume 25 year generation times. $l_{i_g}$ and $l_{j_g}$ are the languages or language families spoken by individuals within genetic clade $g$. $1_{cos(l_{i_g}, l_{i_g}) > 0}$ is 1 if the ith and jth individual share a language, and zero otherwise. $n_g$ is the number of individuals in $g$.

We extend this model to calculate the probability that two individuals share a particular trait, rather than calculating the probability of sharing a trait on average. This allows a more fine-grained view of the language-genetic connection. This approach has been compiled in the function `trait_heritage` within the package `traitheritage`, developed for this project. The trait heritage package can be found at: <https://github.com/SamPassmore/traitheritage>

We calculate the trait heritage for a number of different traits.

-   Whether a language is affiliated with the Trans-New Guinea family or not (`TNG`)
-   Language clade of the individual (`TNG_Branch`)
-   Language of individual (`interview_language`)

As with [@lansing2017], we compare the calculated probability with a permuted probability to determine whether languages are more likely to be shared by chance. We calculate XXX permutations per analysis.

We apply the trait heritage function across a posterior of trees. Within each tree we calculate the probability from the data, and the XXX permutations. This analysis was performed with computational resources provided by NCI Australia, an NCRIS enabled capability supported by the Australian Government.

#### mtDNA N Haplotype

##### Trans-New Guinea structure

```{r echo=FALSE}
mcct_tree_mtdnaN = read.nexus("NCI/20240702_N_CBES_bModelTest/20240617_CBES_bModelTest_adj-papua_n.mcct.trees") 

mcct_depth = mean(adephylo::distRoot(mcct_tree_mtdnaN))

language_probability = 
  read.csv("NCI/20240709_R_N/results/TNG_20240617_CBES_bModelTest_adj-papua_n.noburnin_languagefamily.csv")

# Because we calculate the probability per group, we need to make this generational average 
# for trait probabaility data. But for Permutations, the average is all that is calculated
# because of the computational memory issues. 
language_probability = data.table(language_probability)
language_probability = language_probability[, list(numerator_sum = sum(numerator),
                           denominator_sum = sum(denominator)), 
                           by = list(state, posterior, generation)]
language_probability[, clade_probability := numerator_sum / denominator_sum]
language_probability = language_probability[state == 1,]

permuted_probability = 
  read.csv("NCI/20240709_R_N/results/TNG_20240617_CBES_bModelTest_adj-papua_n.noburnin_permuted_languagefamily.csv")

summarizer = function(posterior){
  posterior$generation_time = as.numeric(gsub("g_", replacement = "", posterior$generation))
  # posterior$clade_probability = posterior$numerator / posterior$numerator
  posterior %>%
  filter(!is.na(clade_probability)) %>% # remove NA clades. Usually occur because of singleton clades
  group_by(generation_time) %>%
  summarise(mean.prob = mean(clade_probability, na.rm = TRUE),
            ci_hdi = bayestestR::ci(clade_probability), # 95% credible interval
            n_matches = sum(numerator_sum)) %>% 
  tidyr::unpack(ci_hdi)
}

# Summarise the posterior
posterior_summary = summarizer(language_probability)
# remove results that are older than the MCCT tree
posterior_summary = posterior_summary[posterior_summary$generation_time < mcct_depth,]

permuted_summary = summarizer(permuted_probability)
permuted_summary = permuted_summary[permuted_summary$generation_time < mcct_depth,]

# cleaned_tips = gsub("_.*","", mcct_tree_mtdnaN$tip.label)
# mcct_tree_mtdnaN$tip.label = cleaned_tips

metadata_ss = metadata[metadata$PhyID %in% mcct_tree_mtdnaN$tip.label, ]
mcct_tree_mtdnaN = keep.tip(mcct_tree_mtdnaN, metadata_ss$PhyID[!is.na(metadata_ss$Branch_Family)])

tree_data = full_join(mcct_tree_mtdnaN, metadata_ss, by = c(label = "PhyID"))

#### plot 
p_tree = ggtree(tree_data) + 
  geom_tippoint(aes(col = TNG), shape = "\u2588", size = 1.0) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(10000, 20000, 30000, 40000),
                     labels = c("10k", "20k", "30k", "40k")) +
  layout_dendrogram() + 
  theme(legend.position = "none", 
        axis.ticks.y = element_line(),
        axis.line.y = element_line(),
        axis.text.y = element_text())

# match scales in each plot
x_range = layer_scales(p_tree)$x$range$range
  
p_prob = ggplot(data = posterior_summary,
                aes(ymin = CI_low, ymax = CI_high, x = generation_time, y = mean.prob)) +
  geom_ribbon(fill = "lightblue", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(col = "blue") +
  geom_ribbon(data = permuted_summary,
              aes(ymin = CI_low, ymax = CI_high, x = generation_time, y = mean.prob),
              fill = "lightgreen", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(data = permuted_summary,
              aes(x = generation_time, y = mean.prob),
            col = "forestgreen") +
  ylim(c(0, 1)) +
  xlim(x_range) + ## max tree height (or max p_tree?)
  coord_flip() +
  xlab("") + 
  ylab("") + 
  # scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) + 
  # scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) + 
  theme_classic() + 
  theme(panel.grid.major = element_blank(), 
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.background = element_rect(colour = "black", linewidth=0.5))

p_tree + p_prob + 
  plot_layout(widths = c(1, 0.25))

```

These next graphs show the probability of shared language family against geographic proximity. we test geographic proximity at three distances: are two individuals within 50km of each other, 100kms, or 200kms.

```{r}
distance50_probability = 
  read.csv("NCI/20240709_R_N/results/TNG_20240617_CBES_bModelTest_adj-papua_n.noburnin_distance50.csv")
distance35_probability = 
  read.csv("NCI/20240709_R_N/results/TNG_20240617_CBES_bModelTest_adj-papua_n.noburnin_distance35.csv")
distance20_probability = 
  read.csv("NCI/20240709_R_N/results/TNG_20240617_CBES_bModelTest_adj-papua_n.noburnin_distance20.csv")

distance_summary = lapply(list(long = distance50_probability,
                        medium = distance35_probability,
                        short = distance20_probability), 
                        summarizer)

distance_summary = bind_rows(distance_summary, .id = "distance")
distance_summary$distance = factor(distance_summary$distance, 
                                   levels = c("short", "medium", "long"))

distance_summary = distance_summary[distance_summary$generation_time < mcct_depth,]

facet_names = c(`short` = "w/n 20km",
                `medium` = "w/n 35km",
                `long` = "w/n 50km")

ggplot(data = distance_summary,
       aes(
         ymin = CI_low,
         ymax = CI_high,
         x = generation_time,
         y = mean.prob
       )) +
  geom_ribbon(fill = "lightgreen", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(data = distance_summary,
            aes(x = generation_time, y = mean.prob),
            col = "forestgreen") +
  facet_grid(~ distance, labeller = as_labeller(facet_names)) +
  geom_ribbon(
    data = posterior_summary,
    aes(
      ymin = CI_low,
      ymax = CI_high,
      x = generation_time,
      y = mean.prob
    ),
    fill = "lightblue",
    alpha = 0.5
  ) + geom_line(data = posterior_summary,
                aes(x = generation_time,
                    y = mean.prob),
                col = "blue") +
  scale_x_reverse(breaks = c(0, 10000, 20000, 30000, 40000, 50000, 60000, 70000),
                  labels = c("0", "10k", "20k", "30k", "40k", "50k", "60k", "70k")) + 
  xlab("Time (years)") + 
  ylab("Probability") + 
  theme_classic()
  

```

#### mtDNA M: By trait results

```{r, eval=FALSE, echo=FALSE}
## Prepare the tree
mcct_tree_mtdnaM = read.nexus("NCI/20240528_mtDNA_CCP/CCP-papua_m_noburnin.mcct.trees")
cleaned_tips = gsub("_.*","", mcct_tree_mtdnaM$tip.label)
mcct_tree_mtdnaM$tip.label = cleaned_tips

metadata_ss = metadata[metadata$ID %in% mcct_tree_mtdnaM$tip.label, ]
mcct_tree_mtdnaM = keep.tip(mcct_tree_mtdnaM, metadata_ss$ID[!is.na(metadata_ss$Branch_Family)])

tree_data = full_join(mcct_tree_mtdnaM, metadata, by = c("label" = "ID"))

## Read in probability data
language_probability = 
  read.csv("results/Branch_Family_CCP-papua_m_noburnin_pruned_languagefamily.csv")

posterior_summary = language_probability %>% 
  mutate(probability = numerator / denominator,
         generation_num = as.numeric(str_remove(generation, "g_"))) %>% 
  group_by(generation_num, posterior) %>% 
  summarise(clade_probability = mean(probability, na.rm = TRUE),
            numerator_sum = sum(numerator)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(clade_probability)) %>% # remove NA clades. Usually occur because of singleton clades
  group_by(generation_num) %>%
  summarise(mean.prob = mean(clade_probability, na.rm = TRUE),
            ci_hdi = bayestestR::ci(clade_probability), # 95% credible interval
            n_matches = sum(numerator_sum)) %>% 
  tidyr::unpack(ci_hdi)

p_tree = ggtree(tree_data) + 
  geom_tippoint(aes(col = Branch_Family), shape = "\u2588", size = 1.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = c(10000, 20000, 30000, 40000),
                     labels = c("10k", "20k", "30k", "40k")) +
  layout_dendrogram() + 
  theme(legend.position = "none", 
        axis.ticks.y = element_line(),
        axis.line.y = element_line(),
        axis.text.y = element_text())

# match scales in each plot
x_range = layer_scales(p_tree)$x$range$range
  
p_prob = ggplot(data = posterior_summary,
                aes(ymin = CI_low, ymax = CI_high, x = generation_num, y = mean.prob)) +
  geom_ribbon(fill = "lightblue", alpha = 0.5) + 
  geom_line(col = "blue") + 
  ylim(c(0, 1)) +
  xlim(x_range) + ## max tree height (or max p_tree?)
  coord_flip() +
  xlab("") + 
  ylab("") + 
  # scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) + 
  # scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) + 
  theme_classic() + 
  theme(panel.grid.major = element_blank(), 
        panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
        panel.background = element_rect(colour = "black", linewidth=0.5))

pp = p_tree + p_prob + 
  plot_layout(widths = c(1, 0.25))

ggsave(plot = pp, filename = "figures/mtDNA_M_CCP_wprob.png", width = 1920, units = "px", height = 1080)
```

## Stable Clades

We further test the correlation between linguistic affiliation and genetic clades by testing trait stability across the posterior sample of trees. To do this, each individual within a phylogeny is assigned a trait. For a particular phylogeny, we identify all genetic clades where the trait is the same between all individuals. We then look across the posterior of phylogeny and identify clades that exist in more than 50% of the posterior (i.e. are stable clades).

#### mtDNA N Haplotypes

```{r eval = FALSE, echo=FALSE}
if(!file.exists("results/mtDNA_N_stableclades.csv")){
  system("RScript analysis/stable_clades.R -t NCI/20240702_N_CBES_bModelTest/20240617_CBES_bModelTest_adj-papua_n.noburnin.trees -v TNG")
}

## Metadata 
metadata = read.csv("processed_data/genetic_samples.csv")

stable_clades_summary = read.csv("results/mtDNA_N_stableclades_summary.csv")

states_df = data.frame(states = metadata$Branch_Family, label = metadata$ID)
states_df = left_join(states_df, metadata[, c("ID", "gender")], by = c("label" = "ID"))

mcct_tree_mtdnaN = read.nexus("NCI/mtDNA_N/mtDNA_N-papua_n_daru_pruned.mcct.trees")

# clean IDs
metadata$ID = gsub("-.*","", metadata$ID)

# subset to taxa in the phylogeny
metadata_ss = metadata[metadata$ID %in% mcct_tree_mtdnaN$tip.label,]

# extract the trait of interest
trait = metadata_ss$Branch_Family
trait[trait == ""] = NA
names(trait) = metadata_ss$ID

# remove missing traits
trait = trait[!is.na(trait)]
trait_df = data.frame(states = factor(trait), label = names(trait))

# match traits and tips
plot_tree = keep.tip(mcct_tree_mtdnaN, names(trait))
plot_tree = ladderize(plot_tree)

nodes = sapply(stable_clades_summary$tips, function(x)
  phytools::findMRCA(plot_tree, tips = unlist(strsplit(x, "; ")))) %>% 
  as.data.frame()
colnames(nodes) = "node"
nodes$tips = rownames(nodes)

# nodes_df = data.frame(nodes = nodes, type = stable_clades_summary$state)
nodes_df = left_join(stable_clades_summary, nodes, by = "tips")

tree_df = tidytree::left_join(plot_tree, trait_df, by = "label") 

## set colours
family_colours = setNames(scales::hue_pal()(17), levels(trait_df$states))

p1 = ggtree(tree_df, layout="roundrect", ladderize = TRUE, mrsd = "2023-01-01") + 
  # geom_tippoint(aes(colour = states), shape = "\u25ac", size = 4.0) +
  geom_tippoint(aes(colour = states), size = 1.0) +
  geom_hilight(data = nodes_df, aes(node = node, fill = state),
               type = "roundrect",
               to.bottom = FALSE) +
  labs(title = "N Haplotypes") + 
  theme_classic(base_size = 20) + 
  scale_color_manual(values = family_colours) + 
  scale_fill_manual(values = family_colours) + 
  guides(color=guide_legend(element_blank()), fill = "none") + 
  theme_tree2() + 
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
p1
ggsave(plot = p1, filename = "figures/stable_clades.pdf")
```

### Pairwise Between & Within group variance

We do not only want to understand the probability of particular histories, but also rate at which histories coalesce. To do this, for each pair we calculate the probability of between and within group variance to understand at what point, according to the phylogeny, were two languages groups likely to have been one language group.

This approach extends some assumptions of the phylogenetic model. First, that all partitions are binary.

```{r}
metadata_ss = metadata[metadata$ID %in% mcct_tree_mtdnaN, ]
trait = metadata_ss$TNG
names(trait) = metadata_ss$ID

# w_b = traitheritage::within_between(tree = mcct_tree_mtdnaM, generation_time = 25, trait = trait)
# 
# saveRDS(w_b, "results/Branch_Family_mtDNAM_CCP_withinbetween.RDS")
# w_b = readRDS("results/Branch_Family_mtDNAM_CCP_withinbetween.RDS")

w_b = 
  readRDS("NCI/20240709_R_N/results/TNG_20240617_CBES_bModelTest-papua_n.noburnin_withinbetween.RDS")
v_within = lapply(w_b, '[[', "v_within")
v_within = rbindlist(v_within, idcol = "tree")
v_within[,  generation_num := as.numeric(str_remove(generation, "g_")),]
v_within = v_within[generation_num < mcct_depth,]
setkey(v_within, trait)

v_within_av = v_within[, 
                .(v_within_av = mean(v_within)), 
                       by = list(trait, generation_num)]

v_within_er = v_within[,
                       .(CI_Low = unlist(bayestestR::ci(v_within)["CI_low"]),
                         CI_High = unlist(bayestestR::ci(v_within)["CI_high"])),
                       by = list(trait, generation_num)]

v_within_av = bind_cols(v_within_av, v_within_er[,c("CI_Low", "CI_High")])

# kainantu_chumbu_w = v_within[J(c("Chimbu-Wahgi", "Kainantu-Goroka"))]

v_between = lapply(w_b, '[[', "v_between")
v_between = rbindlist(v_between, idcol = "tree")
v_between[,  generation_num := as.numeric(str_remove(generation, "g_")),]
v_between = v_between[generation_num < mcct_depth,]
setkey(v_between, trait_pairs)

v_between_av = v_between[,
                         .(v_between_av = mean(v_between)),

v_between_er = v_between[,

# kainantu_chumbu_b = v_between[J(c("Chimbu-WahgiKainantu-Goroka"))]

ggplot() + 
  geom_line(data = v_within_av, aes(x = generation_num, y = v_within_av, col = trait)) + 
  geom_ribbon(data = v_within_av,
              aes(ymin = CI_Low, ymax = CI_High, x = generation_num, y = v_within_av, fill = trait),

  geom_line(data = v_between_av, aes(x = generation_num, y = v_between_av), col = "forestgreen") +

              aes(ymin = CI_Low, ymax = CI_High, x = generation_num, y = v_between_av),
              fill = "lightgreen", alpha = 0.5) 

ggplot() +

              aes(ymin = CI_Low, ymax = CI_High, x = generation_num, y = v_within_av, fill = trait),
```
